title: PagedAttention and prefix caching
summary: How vLLM pages the KV cache into blocks, reads them in its attention kernel, shares them with copy-on-write, reuses cached prefixes by chained hashes or a radix tree, and keeps hits across a fleet.
outcomes: Explain why contiguous max-length KV allocation wastes memory and limits batch size
Trace how a block table maps logical KV blocks to physical blocks during prefill and decode
Explain how the PagedAttention kernel lays out keys for contiguous loads and merges partitions exactly
Compute memory saved by sharing prompt blocks with reference counts and copy-on-write
Predict which prompt tokens hit vLLM's prefix cache using chained block hashes and LRU eviction
Show why a prefix hit saves prefill but not decode reads, and how cascade attention reads a prefix once
Compare RadixAttention with hash-based caching and judge when prefix caching pays off
Estimate how routing across replicas changes the hit rate, and order prompts to keep hits

lessons.title: Recap: why the vLLM paper paged the KV cache

blocks.md:
Recall from the prerequisite course (LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management): decoding keeps every token's key and value vectors in GPU memory, the batch size is capped by how many of those KV caches fit, and older servers wasted most of that memory by reserving one contiguous max-length chunk per request. This short lesson keeps only the vLLM paper's own numbers, because later lessons build on them.

The vLLM paper (Kwon et al., SOSP 2023, the Symposium on Operating Systems Principles) measured a 13B-parameter model on a 40 GB NVIDIA A100: about 65% of memory holds the weights, which never change, and close to 30% holds the KV cache. So the way the KV cache is managed decides the batch size.

blocks.caption: KV cache per token for OPT-13B, the paper's own example. At the model's 2048-token maximum, one request can need about 1.68 GB.

blocks.md: In the paper's setup (Table 1), OPT-13B on one A100 leaves 12 GB for the KV cache, which is about 15,728 token slots: 12 GB, counted as 12 x 1024 x 1024 x 1024 bytes, divided by 819,200 bytes per token. FasterTransformer and Orca stored each request's KV cache as one contiguous tensor sized for its maximum possible length, which wastes slots three ways (reserved, internal fragmentation, external fragmentation; the prerequisite course's lesson on fragmentation and block tables walks through each). The paper measured how much of the KV memory ended up holding real token states:

blocks.title: Share of KV memory holding actual token states

scenes.caption: Measured in the vLLM paper (Fig. 2). Orca variants reserve the model maximum, up to 2x the true output, or exactly the true output (an impossible oracle). Even the oracle wastes most memory to fragmentation.

blocks.prompt: Simplified model: 15.7K slots, every request reserves the 2048-token maximum, versus an allocator that only spends what a request actually uses. ShareGPT requests (shared ChatGPT chats) in the paper average about 499 tokens (input plus output). Roughly how many requests fit in each case?
blocks.reveal:
Contiguous at maximum length: 15,728 / 2048 = **7** requests. Allocating only what is used, with at most a few slots of slack each: about 15,728 / 507 = **31** requests, over 4x more. The 507 is the 499 average tokens plus about 8 slots of slack, the average unfilled tail of a 16-token block (lesson 2 derives it).

This back-of-the-envelope estimate ignores that live requests are only partly grown, but it lands near the paper's measurement: vLLM batched 4.3x more requests than Orca (Max) on OPT-13B with ShareGPT.

blocks.title: Requests that fit in a 15,728-slot KV pool

scenes.caption: Reserving the 2048-token maximum fits 15,728 / 2048 = 7 requests, however few tokens each one really uses: the curve is flat.
Allocating 16-token blocks only as tokens arrive costs each request its length plus on average 7.5 empty slots in its last block. At the ShareGPT average of 499 tokens, 31 requests fit.
With 128-token blocks the last block wastes 63.5 slots on average, which costs little at 2,000 tokens but a lot at 150. Lesson 2 derives that average and the paper's choice of 16.

blocks.md: Decoding is memory-bound: each step reads all the weights and every request's KV cache from GPU memory to produce just one token per request, so memory traffic, not arithmetic, sets the step time. A bigger batch reuses the same weight reads for more requests, so throughput comes from batch size, and batch size comes from how many KV caches fit. Any slot that is reserved, fragmented, or duplicated is a request you could not batch.

Knowing the exact output length would not fix this. Orca (Oracle) assumes perfect knowledge and still stores real token states in only 38.2% of KV memory, because contiguous chunks of different sizes still fragment the space and still cannot be shared.

blocks.question: Which change would most increase batch size for a contiguous-allocation server?
options: Use a faster attention kernel
Increase the maximum sequence length so fewer requests are rejected
Allocate KV memory in small fixed-size pieces on demand instead of one max-length chunk per request
Sort waiting requests by prompt length before batching them
blocks.explain: Waste comes from reserving for the worst case in one contiguous piece. Allocating small fixed-size pieces only when tokens arrive removes reservation and external fragmentation and caps internal fragmentation at one piece per sequence. That is exactly PagedAttention's design.

lessons.title: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache

blocks.md:
The prerequisite course introduced block tables as page tables for the KV cache. This lesson follows the vLLM paper's own version closely, because the next lesson opens the kernel that reads it.

PagedAttention borrows the operating system's answer to fragmentation: **paging**. The paper's analogy is direct: KV blocks are pages, tokens are bytes, and requests are processes.

A **KV block** holds the keys and values of a fixed number of tokens, the **block size** $B$. A request sees its KV cache as a list of *logical* blocks, filled left to right. A per-request **block table** maps each logical block to a *physical* block anywhere in a pool that the engine carves out of GPU memory at startup. Each entry also records how many slots are filled.

blocks.title: Block table translation (block size 4)

scenes.caption: Prefill of request A, prompt "Four score and seven years ago our" (7 tokens). Only 2 blocks are allocated, not the maximum length: logical 0 maps to physical 7, logical 1 to physical 1. Logical 1 has one free slot.
First decode step: the new token "fathers" goes into the free slot of logical block 1. No allocation happens; only the filled count changes.
Second decode step: logical block 1 is full, so the manager grabs any free physical block (here 3) for logical block 2. Logically contiguous, physically scattered.
A second request B with a 6-token prompt gets physical blocks 5 and 2. Both requests share one pool; each wastes at most the unfilled tail of its last block.

blocks.md: Request A's first three scenes follow Fig. 6 of the paper. Because a new physical block is allocated only when the previous one is full, the waste per sequence is bounded by one partly filled block. Every block has the same size, so there is no external fragmentation: any free block fits any request.

blocks.title: Translating a token position to a physical slot
blocks.code:
B = 4                   # tokens per block
table = [7, 1, 3]       # request A: entry i = physical block of logical block i

def slot(pos):
    blk, off = divmod(pos, B)
    return table[blk] * B + off

for pos in [0, 5, 8]:
    print(pos, slot(pos))

scenes.caption: Position 0 is in logical block 0, offset 0. The table sends it to physical block 7, slot 28 of the pool.
Position 5 ("ago") is logical block 1, offset 1. Physical block 1 starts at slot 4, so the slot is 5.
Position 8 ("brought") is logical block 2, offset 0, which lives in physical block 3: slot 12. The kernel does this lookup on the fly; lesson 3 shows how.

blocks.md: Attention itself is rewritten block by block. Number the blocks from 1: key block $K_j$ and value block $V_j$ hold the keys and values of tokens $(j-1)B+1$ to $jB$, stored as the $B$ columns of a matrix. The query of token $i$ is scored against one block at a time, wherever that block lives:

blocks.tex: A_{ij}=\frac{\exp\left(q_i^\top K_j/\sqrt{d}\right)}{\sum_{t=1}^{\lceil i/B\rceil}\exp\left(q_i^\top K_t/\sqrt{d}\right)\mathbf{1}},\qquad o_i=\sum_{j=1}^{\lceil i/B\rceil} V_j A_{ij}^\top
blocks.caption: Eq. 4 of the vLLM paper. exp acts on each of the B scores separately, and the all-ones vector 1 adds them up. The paper writes the 1 inside the exp; it is moved out here so the sum is explicit. The result equals ordinary attention.

blocks.md: In words: $q_i^\top K_j$ is a row of $B$ scores, one per key in block $j$, each divided by $\sqrt{d}$, where $d$ is the length of a key vector. $A_{ij}$ is that row after exponentiating and dividing by the sum of all exponentiated scores in blocks 1 to $\lceil i/B \rceil$, the block that holds token $i$. Laid side by side, the $A_{ij}$ of all blocks are the usual softmax over earlier tokens, cut into pieces of $B$. The output $o_i$ adds each value block's vectors weighted by its piece. Slots after token $i$ in its own block are masked out, which the equation leaves implicit.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
q = np.array([1.0, 0.0])                      # one query, d = 2
K = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1], [2, 0]], float)  # 4 keys
V = np.array([10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0])        # scalar values
blocks = [[0, 1], [2, 3]]                     # B = 2: two KV blocks

# ordinary attention over all 4 keys
s = K @ q / np.sqrt(2)
print("scores", s.round(3))
w = np.exp(s) / np.exp(s).sum()
print("ordinary output", round(float(w @ V), 4))

# Eq. 4: score one block at a time, then normalise by the
# sum over all blocks (exp(q K_t / sqrt d) 1 = block t's exp-score sum)
num, den = 0.0, 0.0
for j, idx in enumerate(blocks):
    e = np.exp(K[idx] @ q / np.sqrt(2))       # exp scores of block j
    print(f"block {j}: exp scores {e.round(3)}, block sum {e.sum():.3f}")
    num += e @ V[idx]
    den += e.sum()
print("blockwise output", round(num / den, 4))
blocks.caption: A numeric check with one query and two blocks of 2 keys (d = 2, scalar values for readability). Runs with Python 3 and NumPy.

blocks.code:
scores [0.707 0.    0.707 1.414]
ordinary output 28.9716
block 0: exp scores [2.028 1.   ], block sum 3.028
block 1: exp scores [2.028 4.113], block sum 6.141
blockwise output 28.9716
blocks.caption: Output of a real run. Each block contributes its exp scores and their sum; dividing the summed weighted values by 3.028 + 6.141 gives the same 28.9716 as one softmax over all four keys.

blocks.title: Expected KV waste per sequence: paged vs reserve-max

scenes.caption: Simplified model: the last block holds 1 to B tokens with equal odds, so on average (B-1)/2 slots sit empty. With B = 16 a 500-token sequence wastes about 1.5%, while reserving 2048 slots wastes 76%.

With B = 128 short sequences waste much more: the paper saw large blocks hurt on Alpaca (an instruction-following dataset of short prompts and answers), whose sequences are often shorter than one block.
B = 1 wastes nothing but forces the kernel to fetch one token at a time. The paper found 16 large enough for GPU efficiency and small enough for low waste, and made it vLLM's default.

blocks.md: The block table is the whole trick: contiguous logical blocks, scattered physical blocks, allocation on demand. Waste is capped at one partly filled block per sequence.

Paging is not free. The paper measured 20 to 26% higher attention kernel latency than FasterTransformer's kernel, from block-table lookups, extra branches and variable lengths (the next lesson shows where those come from). It still wins end to end because only the attention operator pays, and the larger batch more than makes up for it.

blocks.question: A kernel reads the KV of position `pos` at `base + pos * bytes_per_token`, as a contiguous kernel would. After switching to paged storage, what goes wrong?
options: It reads the right tokens only while the sequence fits in its first block; later positions land in whatever block happens to sit next in memory
Nothing, because physical blocks are allocated in increasing order
It reads correct data but more slowly
It fails only for requests that share blocks
blocks.explain: Logical blocks are mapped to arbitrary physical blocks (7, 1, 3 in the example). Only offsets inside a block are contiguous, so every access must go through the block table: `table[pos // B] * B + pos % B`.

blocks.question: Why does vLLM avoid a block size of 1 even though it minimizes wasted slots?
options: Block tables cannot store more than 1024 entries
Copy-on-write needs at least two tokens per block
Prefix caching only works with block sizes that are powers of two
The kernel processes fewer positions in parallel per fetch, underusing the GPU
blocks.explain: The paper explains that more tokens per block let the PagedAttention kernel process more positions in parallel. Too small underuses the GPU, too large raises internal fragmentation and lowers sharing. 16 was the default it chose.

blocks.md:
Lesson 2 said the kernel looks up the block table "on the fly". Take the 11-token sequence below, stored in physical blocks 5, 2 and 7 of size 4. At every decode step, for every attention head, one new query must be scored against all 11 cached keys and then mix all 11 values, while those keys sit in three places in memory. This lesson opens the CUDA kernel the vLLM paper shipped for that job, then shows how today's kernels do the same thing.

A history note first. vLLM's design docs now mark that walkthrough as historical, and the kernel itself was deleted from the repository in July 2026 (pull request 47361, "Delete PagedAttention"). Paged attention now lives inside vLLM's attention backends. The original is still the clearest example of how to read a paged cache efficiently, and every later design keeps its ideas.

**Layout.** The kernel's key cache has shape `[num_blocks, num_kv_heads, head_size/x, block_size, x]` and its value cache `[num_blocks, num_kv_heads, head_size, block_size]`. Here `x = 16 / sizeof(element)`, which is 8 for FP16 or BF16: one key is cut into chunks of x numbers, exactly 16 bytes, the amount the design doc says a thread group fetches at a time. Within a block, chunk 0 of every token comes first, then chunk 1 of every token, and so on.

Why that order? A GPU runs threads in **warps** of 32 that execute each instruction together; warps are grouped into **thread blocks** that share one streaming multiprocessor's fast on-chip memory, and a kernel launch is a **grid** of thread blocks. Here a **thread group** of 2 threads handles one key token (with block size 16 a warp of 32 threads holds 16 groups, one per token). Each thread loads 4 numbers (8 bytes) at a time, so a group fetches one 16-byte chunk, and the whole warp fetches the same chunk of 16 neighbouring tokens at once.

blocks.title: One key block, two layouts (toy: 4 tokens, 16 numbers each)

scenes.caption: Each cell is one 16-byte chunk of x = 8 FP16 numbers: t2 c1 is chunk 1 of token 2. Top: each token's 16 numbers stored together. Bottom: vLLM's [head_size/x, block_size, x] order, chunk 0 of every token first.
Load 1: each thread group fetches chunk 0 of its own token. In vLLM's order the four fetches are neighbours, one contiguous run; token-major order leaves a gap between every pair.
Load 2: chunk 1 of every token, again one contiguous run in vLLM's order. GPUs serve a warp fastest when its threads read neighbouring addresses (a coalesced access).

Real sizes (block 16, head size 128, FP16): 16 thread groups of 2 threads each fetch chunk j of their token, so the warp reads bytes 0 to 255, then 256 to 511, and so on: 16 contiguous loads per key block.

blocks.md:
**Writing.** Keys and values are written once per new token by `reshape_and_cache`, one GPU thread block per token. The engine passes a **slot mapping**: for each new token, the slot number `block_table[pos // B] * B + pos % B` from lesson 2. The write kernel splits the slot back into a physical block and an offset and scatters the token's key chunks and value numbers into that block's layout. This kernel still exists in current vLLM, with the same tensor shapes in its comments.

The script below rebuilds both layouts in NumPy, writes 11 tokens through a slot mapping, reads them back the way the kernel does, and checks the partitioned result from later in this lesson against plain attention.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
D, BS, X = 16, 4, 8               # head size, block size, x = 16 B / 2 B
kc = np.zeros((8, D // X, BS, X))  # [num_blocks, head_size/x, block_size, x]
vc = np.zeros((8, D, BS))          # [num_blocks, head_size, block_size]
table, L = [5, 2, 7], 11           # block table, tokens (one KV head)
keys, vals = rng.standard_normal((2, L, D))
slots = [table[p // BS] * BS + p % BS for p in range(L)]
print("slot_mapping", slots)
for t, s in enumerate(slots):      # reshape_and_cache
    b, off = divmod(s, BS)
    kc[b, :, off, :] = keys[t].reshape(D // X, X)
    vc[b, :, off] = vals[t]

def read(p):                       # the kernel's lookup for token p
    b, off = table[p // BS], p % BS
    return kc[b, :, off, :].reshape(D), vc[b, :, off]

q = rng.standard_normal(D)
def partial(lo, hi):               # one v2 thread block
    K, V = map(np.array, zip(*[read(p) for p in range(lo, hi)]))
    s = K @ q / 4.0
    e = np.exp(s - s.max())
    return s.max(), e.sum(), e @ V / e.sum()

m, l, o = zip(*[partial(lo, min(lo + 4, L)) for lo in range(0, L, 4)])
r = np.array(l) * np.exp(np.array(m) - max(m))     # reduce kernel
v2 = (np.array(o) * r[:, None]).sum(0) / r.sum()
s = keys @ q / 4.0
w = np.exp(s - s.max())
print("v2 vs dense max err:", np.abs(v2 - w @ vals / w.sum()).max())
blocks.caption: Simplified: one KV head, toy sizes, float64 on the CPU. The layouts and index arithmetic follow vLLM's reshape_and_cache and the original kernel's comments. Runs with Python 3 and NumPy.
Output of a real run: tokens 0 to 3 land in block 5 (slots 20 to 23), 4 to 7 in block 2, 8 to 10 in block 7. The partitioned result matches plain attention to rounding error.

blocks.md:
**Work split.** The kernel launches a grid of `(num_heads, num_seqs, max_num_partitions)` thread blocks of 128 threads each, so one thread block computes one head of one sequence (for one partition). Inside it:

1. Every thread group multiplies the query by its token's key, combining its two halves of the dot product.
2. Each warp walks one KV block at a time: warp w takes logical blocks w, w + 4, w + 8, ..., reading the physical block number from the block table each time.
3. Scores go to shared memory. The block finds the max score and the sum of exponentials with two reductions, then normalises every score.
4. A second walk over the same blocks multiplies value vectors by those scores, and the warps' partial outputs are summed through shared memory.

Each table lookup, the masking of slots past the sequence end, and support for different lengths per sequence are the extra work behind the 20 to 26% kernel overhead from lesson 2.

blocks.title: One thread block of the original kernel (one sequence, one head)

scenes.caption: The grid has one thread block per (head, sequence, partition). Its 128 threads form 4 warps of 32, and all of them share one small, fast on-chip memory (shared memory).

Key pass, for a longer sequence of 5 blocks: warp w reads logical block w, looked up in the block table, so neighbouring blocks come from anywhere in the pool. Inside a warp, each thread group computes one token's score.
With more blocks than warps, warp 0 moves on to logical block 4, then 8, and so on. Scores land in shared memory, one slot per token of the context.

Softmax: threads swap values inside a warp (shuffles) to find the warp's max score, combine the 4 warp maxima through shared memory, then do the same for the sum of exp(score - max) and normalise every score.
Value pass: the warps walk the same blocks again, now multiplying value vectors by the normalised scores. The 4 partial sums are added through shared memory and written out.

blocks.md:
**Version 2: partitions.** With one thread block per (sequence, head), a single 32-head sequence launches only 32 thread blocks, however long its context, while an A100 has 108 streaming multiprocessors (SMs) to fill. So vLLM added a second kernel (v2) that cuts the context into partitions of 512 tokens. Each partition gets its own thread block and writes three things: its max score $m_p$, its sum of exponentials $\ell_p$, and its output $o_p$ normalised within the partition. A small reduce kernel then combines them.

The selection rule in vLLM's old Python wrapper: use v1 when the longest sequence is at most 8,192 tokens and either it fits in one partition or sequences times heads exceeds 512; otherwise use v2. The comment explains that longer contexts always go to v2 to avoid running out of shared memory, which v1 needs for one score per context token.

blocks.caption: The reduce kernel's merge. Rescaling each partition's sum by exp(m_p - M) puts all partitions on the same reference max, so the merged result is exactly the softmax over the whole context.

blocks.title: Merging two partitions exactly (toy numbers)
blocks.code:
scores = [1.0, 2.0, 0.5, 3.0, 1.5, 2.5]   # one query, 6 cached tokens
values = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]         # scalar values for readability
parts = [(0, 3), (3, 6)]                  # toy partition size 3 (real: 512)
m, l, o = [], [], []
for lo, hi in parts:                      # one thread block per partition
    mp = max(scores[lo:hi])
    e = [exp(s - mp) for s in scores[lo:hi]]
    m.append(mp); l.append(sum(e))
    o.append(sum(ei * v for ei, v in zip(e, values[lo:hi])) / sum(e))
M = max(m)                                # reduce kernel
r = [li * exp(mi - M) for li, mi in zip(l, m)]
out = sum(oi * ri for oi, ri in zip(o, r)) / sum(r)

scenes.caption: Partition 0 holds tokens 0 to 2. Its thread block finds the local max 2.0, the sum of exp(s - 2.0) = 1.591, and a locally normalised output 19.0902.
Partition 1 (tokens 3 to 5) runs at the same time in another thread block: max 3.0, sum 1.8297, output 47.8495. Neither block ever sees the other's scores.
The reduce kernel rescales each sum to the global max 3.0: 1.591 x exp(2.0 - 3.0) = 0.5853, while 1.8297 stays. The global sum is 2.415.
Each partition's output is weighted by its share of the global sum: (19.0902 x 0.5853 + 47.8495 x 1.8297) / 2.415 = 40.8793, exactly what one softmax over all 6 tokens gives.

blocks.md: This is the same exact merge that FlashAttention's online softmax uses inside one kernel and that its split-KV decoding uses across thread blocks. For more depth (optional, not a prerequisite), the FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4 course derives it (lesson "Online softmax: exact attention one block at a time") and covers split-KV for decode shapes.

**Today's kernels.** vLLM's docs now say paged attention is implemented inside its attention backends (for example its Triton backend or the FlashAttention-based one) using block tables built by the KV-cache manager. FlashAttention-2's `flash_attn_with_kvcache` accepts a `block_table` (FlashAttention-3 calls it `page_table`) with caches shaped `(num_blocks, page_block_size, nheads_k, headdim)`: token-major, unlike the old split-x key layout. FlashInfer stores the page table in compressed sparse row form: `kv_indptr` marks where each request's pages start, `kv_indices` lists them, and `kv_last_page_len` says how full each last page is.

Bigger pages mean fewer table lookups and longer contiguous reads, at the price of more slack in each last page and coarser sharing. Which page sizes each backend supports, and why, is in the vLLM attention backends course ("KV cache layout and block sizes per backend"); FlashInfer's view of the page table as a block-sparse matrix is in the FlashInfer course.

**An alternative: vAttention** (Prabhu et al., ASPLOS 2025) keeps each request's KV cache *virtually* contiguous and maps physical memory only as it fills, using CUDA's virtual memory management APIs. Virtual address space is plentiful, so it reserves a max-size region per request slot up front; physical pages are attached on demand. Unmodified non-paged kernels then just work: it ran FlashAttention-3, which was released without paging support, as is.

The costs move elsewhere. CUDA maps memory in 2 MB pages, so the authors modified the open-source part of NVIDIA's driver to allow 64 KB pages, and every mapping is a slow call into the driver, which they hide by allocating in a background thread one step ahead. They report up to 1.99x higher decode throughput than vLLM's paged kernel, but FlashAttention-2's own paged kernel gains as much: the gap is kernel quality, and they find paged and non-paged decode kernels about equally fast. Against those paged kernels the gain is up to 1.18x (FlashAttention-2) and 1.23x (FlashInfer) end to end in long-context runs (A100; not run here).

Paging does not make attention read fewer bytes. Every token's key and value are still loaded once per decode step per head; the layout only decides whether those loads are long contiguous runs or scattered pieces, and how many table lookups and masks wrap around them.

A paged kernel is ordinary attention plus indirection: a table lookup per block, a layout chosen so a warp's loads are contiguous, and, for long contexts, partitions merged exactly with a max-and-sum rescale.

blocks.question: A 32-head model decodes one request with a 32,000-token context on a GPU with 108 SMs. Why does the v2 kernel, with 512-token partitions, help here?
options: It reads fewer KV bytes, because partitions skip tokens with low scores
v1 launches one thread block per head, only 32, so most SMs sit idle; v2 launches about 63 per head, roughly 2,000 in total, to spread the 32,000 keys over the whole GPU
It avoids computing the softmax, which is the slow part at long contexts
It lets heads share one copy of the keys
blocks.explain: v1's grid is (heads, sequences), so batch 1 gives 32 thread blocks, each walking 32,000 keys alone. v2 adds a partition dimension: ceil(32000/512) = 63 partitions per head. The reduce kernel's merge is exact, and the old selection rule sends any context over 8,192 tokens to v2 anyway.

blocks.question: Why did vLLM's original key cache split each key into x-number chunks, with shape [..., head_size/x, block_size, x]?
options: To quantize keys to 8 bits
Because the head size must be a multiple of the block size
So the reduce kernel can merge partitions without shared memory
So a warp, with one thread group per token, reads the same 16-byte chunk of all 16 tokens in a block as one contiguous 256-byte run
blocks.explain: x = 16 / element size, so one chunk is one 16-byte load. Placing chunk j of every token in the block next to each other makes the warp's 16 simultaneous loads touch neighbouring addresses, which the GPU serves as a coalesced access. Token-major order would place them 256 bytes apart, one 16-byte piece per 256-byte row.

blocks.question: Which of these is a real cost of vAttention compared with PagedAttention?
options: It needs attention kernels rewritten to follow a block table
Its results differ slightly from exact attention
Physical memory is attached through driver calls in pages of 64 KB to 2 MB, so each mapping is slow and has to be hidden in a background thread, and allocation is coarser than 16-token blocks
It keeps the KV cache in CPU memory
blocks.explain: Rewriting kernels is PagedAttention's cost, which vAttention avoids. vAttention's costs are driver-level: CUDA's mapping calls are slow, so it allocates one step ahead in the background, and pages are coarse: one layer's key buffer for Llama 3 8B takes 2 KiB per token, so a 2 MB page (stock CUDA) holds 1,024 tokens and even a 64 KB page (the authors' driver change) holds 32.

lessons.title: Sharing blocks with reference counts and copy-on-write

blocks.md:
Paging also makes **sharing** cheap. In *parallel sampling* one prompt produces several outputs, so every output sequence starts with the same prompt KV. With a block table, two sequences can simply point their logical blocks at the same physical blocks.

To know when a shared block can be freed or modified, each physical block keeps a **reference count**: how many logical blocks map to it. vLLM borrows **copy-on-write** from OS process forking: a block with a count above 1 is copied before anyone writes into it.

blocks.title: Parallel sampling: share the prompt, copy on write

scenes.caption: Prefill runs once for the shared prompt. Both samples map logical blocks 0 and 1 to physical blocks 7 and 1, so each has reference count 2. One copy of the prompt KV serves both.
A1 samples "fathers" and must write it into its logical block 1. That physical block is shared (ref 2), so writing in place would corrupt A2's context.
Copy-on-write: allocate physical 3, copy block 1 into it, point A1 at it, and drop block 1's count to 1. A1 then writes "fathers" into its private copy.
A2 samples "mothers". Block 1 now has count 1, so A2 writes in place with no copy. Only the last, partly filled prompt block was ever duplicated.

blocks.prompt: A request asks for 4 samples of a 100-token prompt, each generating 50 tokens, with block size 16. How many blocks are needed without sharing, and with prompt sharing plus copy-on-write?
blocks.reveal:
Without sharing: each sequence has 150 tokens, so ceil(150/16) = 10 blocks, times 4 = **40**.

With sharing: the 6 full prompt blocks (96 tokens) are stored once. Each sample then owns its remaining 54 tokens (4 prompt tokens in the copied last block plus 50 new ones): ceil(54/16) = 4 blocks each. Total 6 + 4 x 4 = **22**, a 45% saving.

blocks.md:
**Beam search** shares even more. Recall that beam search keeps the k most likely partial outputs alive and extends each by one token per step. Beam candidates share the prompt and often long stretches of generated text, and the sharing pattern changes every step as candidates are dropped and forked, like a process tree. When a candidate is dropped, vLLM decrements the counts of its blocks and frees any that reach 0. Older systems had to copy large parts of one candidate's KV into another; vLLM copies at most one block.

The paper's engine supports all of these with three operations on sequences: `fork`, `append` and `free`. The figure below runs all three on a beam of width 2.

Current vLLM (its V1 engine) has no such sequence operations. It runs parallel sampling as n separate requests and beam search as a loop of one-token requests driven from outside the engine; they share blocks through prefix caching (next lesson), which shares only full blocks, so there is no copy-on-write and no gang scheduling.

blocks.title: Beam search, width 2: fork, append, free (block size 4)

scenes.caption: The 4-token prompt fills physical block 0. fork gives the two beam candidates b0 and b1 the same block: reference count 2, 1 block in use.
Step 1: block 0 is full, so each candidate's append opens a private block (1 and 2). Nothing is copied. 3 blocks in use.
Step 2: both best continuations extend b0. free(b1) drops block 2 to 0 and recycles it. fork(b0) creates b2, which shares blocks 0 and 1: both now have count 2.
b0 appends first. Block 1 is shared and only partly full, so copy-on-write copies it to block 3, the only copy so far. b2 then owns block 1 alone and writes in place.

Step 3: both append in place. Still 3 blocks and 1 copy; with private copies the pair would hold 4 blocks. b0 and b2 share block 0, so the paper's vLLM preempts and resumes them together as one group.

blocks.code:
B = 4                                   # tokens per block
free, ref, copies = list(range(8)), {}, 0
seqs = {}                               # name -> [blocks, n_tokens]

def alloc():
    b = free.pop(0); ref[b] = 1; return b

def fork(src, dst):                     # share every block, bump counts
    seqs[dst] = [list(seqs[src][0]), seqs[src][1]]
    for b in seqs[dst][0]: ref[b] += 1

def append(s):                          # write one token
    global copies
    blocks, n = seqs[s]
    if n % B == 0:                      # last block full: new block
        blocks.append(alloc())
    elif ref[blocks[-1]] > 1:           # shared partial block: copy-on-write
        ref[blocks[-1]] -= 1; blocks[-1] = alloc(); copies += 1
    seqs[s][1] = n + 1

def drop(s):                            # free: decrement, recycle at 0
    for b in seqs.pop(s)[0]:
        ref[b] -= 1
        if ref[b] == 0: del ref[b]; free.append(b)

seqs["b0"] = [[alloc()], 4]             # 4-token prompt fills block 0
fork("b0", "b1")
for step, (keep, extend) in enumerate([(["b0", "b1"], ["b0", "b1"]),
                                       (["b0"], ["b0", "b2"]),
                                       (["b0", "b2"], ["b0", "b2"])], 1):
    for s in list(seqs):
        if s not in keep: drop(s)
    for s in extend:
        if s not in seqs: fork("b0", s)
    for s in extend: append(s)
    print(f"step {step}:", {s: v[0] for s, v in seqs.items()},
          "refs", ref, "blocks used", len(ref), "copies", copies)
blocks.caption: The three operations as a tiny allocator: reference counts, a free list, and copy-on-write on a shared, partly filled last block. It replays the figure above.

scenes.caption: Low end of the ranges in the paper (blocks saved by sharing divided by blocks needed without sharing), across numbers of samples or beam widths.
High end of the ranges. Beam search saves far more because candidates share generated tokens too, and ShareGPT's longer prompts make sharing pay more.

blocks.md: **When memory runs out**, the paper's vLLM preempts whole sequences, all of their blocks at once, latest arrivals first, and treats the sequences of one request (beam candidates, parallel samples) as a group that is preempted and resumed together because they may share blocks. The evicted KV comes back by swapping or recomputation; the prerequisite course's lesson on admission control and preemption covers both.
A physical block may back many logical blocks. Reference counts say when it can be freed; copy-on-write makes writes into shared blocks safe, at the cost of copying one block.

blocks.question: Two samples share physical block 9 (ref 2) as their last prompt block. Sample 1 writes first, then sample 2. How many block copies happen?
options: Two, one per sample
One: sample 1 copies, which leaves block 9 with ref 1, so sample 2 writes in place
Zero, because writes to the last block are always private
One, but sample 2 makes it because it writes second
blocks.explain: Copy-on-write triggers only when the count is above 1. Sample 1 sees ref 2, copies into a new block and decrements block 9 to 1. Sample 2 then owns block 9 alone and writes in place, exactly as in the paper's Fig. 8.

blocks.question: Why does vLLM evict all of a sequence's blocks at once instead of picking the least recently used blocks like an OS?
options: Every decode step attends over all of the sequence's earlier tokens, so a partially evicted sequence cannot run anyway
GPU memory only supports freeing whole requests
LRU needs timestamps that GPUs cannot record
Partial eviction would break the block size invariant
blocks.explain: Attention reads every previous token's KV, so a sequence with any block missing cannot take its next step. The paper therefore evicts all or none of a sequence's blocks, and gang-schedules sequences that share blocks, such as beam candidates.

lessons.title: Automatic prefix caching in vLLM: hashing full blocks

blocks.md:
Many requests start with the same tokens: a long system prompt, few-shot examples (worked examples placed in the prompt to show the task), a document asked about repeatedly, or the history of a chat. The KV of a token depends only on the tokens before it, so two requests with the same prefix have identical KV for that prefix. Recomputing it is pure waste.

The PagedAttention paper already handled this with prefixes *reserved by the operator in advance*, like shared libraries in an OS. **Automatic prefix caching (APC)** in vLLM does it with no configuration: it keeps the KV blocks of past requests and reuses them whenever a new request starts the same way. Current vLLM turns it on by default for models that support it; `enable_prefix_caching` sets it explicitly.

The key question is how to find a cached block quickly. vLLM gives each **full** block a hash computed from three things: the hash of the previous block (the *parent*), the block's own tokens, and extra keys that make it unique, such as a LoRA adapter ID, image hashes for multimodal inputs, or a cache salt.

A LoRA adapter fine-tunes a shared base model by adding the product of two small, thin matrices (which is what low rank refers to) to some of its weight matrices, so the same tokens give different KV under different adapters and must not share blocks. A cache salt is an optional string a client attaches to a request so that only requests with the same salt can share cached blocks; the tip at the end of this lesson explains why.

blocks.tex: h_0=\mathrm{H}(\varnothing,\ t_{0..B-1},\ e),\qquad h_i=\mathrm{H}(h_{i-1},\ t_{iB..(i+1)B-1},\ e)
blocks.caption: In words: block 0 hashes an empty parent, its B tokens and the extra keys e; block i hashes the previous block's hash, its own B tokens and e. Chaining the parent hash makes block i's hash identify the entire prefix up to the end of block i, not just its own tokens.

blocks.title: Chained block hashes (simplified, block size 4)
blocks.code:
import hashlib

def block_hash(parent, tokens):
    key = repr((parent, tuple(tokens))).encode()
    return hashlib.sha256(key).hexdigest()[:8]

blocks = [["A", "gentle", "breeze", "stirred"],
          ["the", "leaves", "as", "children"],
          ["laughed", "in", "the", "distance"]]
parent = None
for toks in blocks:
    parent = block_hash(parent, toks)
    print(parent)

scenes.caption: Block 0 has no parent, so its hash depends only on its 4 tokens. (vLLM itself hashes token IDs plus extra keys with sha256 by default; this toy hashes the words.)
Block 1's hash mixes in block 0's hash, so it stands for all 8 tokens so far.
Block 2's hash identifies all 12 tokens. A lookup table from hash to physical block now finds any cached prefix one block at a time.

blocks.prompt: Another request is identical except that "children" becomes "kids". Block 2 ("laughed in the distance") has exactly the same tokens as before. Will its block 2 hit the cache?
blocks.reveal:
No. Block 0 still hashes to `d203e4d2` and hits. Block 1 changes to `0a432e57`, and because block 2's hash includes its parent, it becomes `1eb8b515` instead of `09c07380`.

That is the correct behavior: block 2's keys and values were computed while attending to "kids", so they really are different. Matching stops at the first block that differs.

blocks.md: Only **full** blocks are cached. If two prompts share 10 tokens and the block size is 16, nothing is reused. Lookup also always starts from block 0: a shared passage in the middle of two prompts gives no hit, because its KV depends on everything before it.

**Data structures.** All blocks are created up front as a block pool. A *free queue* (a doubly linked list threaded through the blocks) holds every block with reference count 0, in eviction order; a dictionary maps hashes to cached blocks. Freeing a block does **not** erase its KV: it goes to the tail of the free queue still cached. New allocations pop from the head, and if that block is cached, its hash is dropped then. This is LRU eviction.

The example below is the one in the vLLM design docs: block size 4, 10 blocks, rows show owner, reference count, a short form of each cached hash (computed by our toy hash), and the free queue from head to tail.

blocks.title: vLLM block pool with prefix caching (10 blocks, size 4)

scenes.caption: Time 1: request R0 brings 15 prompt tokens. With block size 4 it gets blocks 0 to 3 from the head of the free queue. Blocks 0, 1, 2 are full, so they are hashed and cached; block 3 holds 3 tokens and is not.
Time 2: R0 decodes. Its 16th token fills block 3, which is now hashed and cached; its next token needs a new block, so block 4 is popped from the queue.
Time 3: R1 has 14 prompt tokens, the first 10 equal to R0's. Only blocks 0 and 1 (8 tokens) hit: block 2 matches just 2 of its 4 tokens. Hit blocks get ref 2; R1 computes only 6 tokens.
Time 4: R0 finishes. Blocks 0 and 1 stay in use by R1. Blocks 4, 3, 2 return to the free queue tail in reverse order, still holding their cached KV and hashes.
Time 5: R1 finishes; blocks 6, 5, 1, 0 go to the tail. Every block is free, yet 5 of them still hold reusable KV. Free and cached are not exclusive.
Time 6: R2 (29 tokens, first 12 equal to R0's) hits blocks 0, 1, 2, which are pulled out of the queue. It needs 5 more and pops 7, 8, 9, 4, 3. Block 3 still held R0's cached KV, so it is evicted.

blocks.md: Two details in that trace are deliberate. Hit blocks are *touched* first: their count rises and they leave the free queue, so the allocation that follows cannot evict the very blocks it just matched (blocks 0, 1, 2 at time 6). And a finished request's blocks enter the queue in reverse order, because the last block of a request covers the longest prefix and is the least likely to be reused, so it should be evicted first.

A cache hit needs the whole prefix up to a block boundary to match. Chained hashes make that a sequence of dictionary lookups, and keeping freed blocks cached until they are actually reallocated makes eviction LRU for free.

For multi-tenant servers (one server shared by many users or customers), give each user or trust group its own `cache_salt`. vLLM mixes it into the first block's hash only, and because every later hash chains from its parent, all of the request's block hashes change with it. This blocks timing attacks where one user detects another's cached prompt by its faster first token. The default hash is sha256; faster non-cryptographic options exist but raise collision risk.

**In practice: what bypasses or limits a hit.** Read from vLLM's KV-cache manager and request code:

- A request that asks for **prompt logprobs** (the probability of every prompt token) reads nothing from the cache by default, because every prompt position must be computed to score it. Pooling models that pool over all tokens skip it too.
- The **last prompt token is always recomputed**, because its forward pass produces the logits for the first output token. The next lesson shows what that does at block boundaries.
- **Multimodal inputs** are safe rather than skipped: image or audio placeholder tokens look identical, so each block's extra keys include the item's identifier and its offset in the block.
- **Hybrid models** change what a hit means. For sliding-window layers a hit needs only the last window of tokens still cached; Mamba layers keep their state only at block boundaries. vLLM intersects the hits of the full-attention group and the other group (its hybrid KV cache manager design doc).

**Seeing the hit rate.** vLLM exports two counters on its `/metrics` endpoint for Prometheus (a monitoring system that scrapes such counters and queries them with its PromQL language), `vllm:prefix_cache_queries` and `vllm:prefix_cache_hits`, both counted in tokens (Prometheus exposes them with a `_total` suffix). Its metrics design doc explains why they are counters rather than a hit-rate gauge: you choose the window, for example hits over queries in the last 5 minutes with PromQL's `rate()`. The periodic log line also prints a recent hit rate.

To check a deployment by hand, send the same long prompt twice and compare time to first token: the second request should skip almost all of its prefill.

blocks.question: Block size 16. Request X has a 100-token prompt. Request Y shares X's first 40 tokens, then differs. With X's blocks still cached, how many of Y's prompt tokens are reused?
options: 0, because the prompts differ
blocks.explain: Only full blocks that match from the start are reused. Tokens 0 to 15 and 16 to 31 form two matching full blocks; the third block (32 to 47) contains differing tokens, so its hash differs. 2 x 16 = 32 tokens are reused; the other 8 shared tokens are recomputed.

blocks.question: At time 6 of the trace, why was block 3 evicted while cached block 5 survived?
options: Block 3 had the oldest hash
Block 5 belonged to R1, which has higher priority
Block 3 was nearer the head of the free queue, and allocation pops from the head
Block 5 was full and block 3 was not
blocks.explain: Eviction is just popping the free queue's head. After the hits were removed the queue read 7, 8, 9, 4, 3, 6, 5, and R2 needed 5 blocks, so 3 was the last one taken and its hash was dropped. Block 5 survived only because it sat further back in the queue; age of the hash and owner do not matter.

blocks.question: Which of these requests reads nothing from vLLM's prefix cache by default, even if its whole prompt is cached?
options: A request that uses a LoRA adapter
A request that asks for prompt logprobs
A request that contains an image
A request that sets a cache_salt
blocks.explain: Prompt logprobs need a forward pass over every prompt position, so the request's cache-hit limit is 0 by default. LoRA, images and salts only change the block hashes: such requests still hit blocks made under the same adapter, image or salt.

lessons.title: Prefill on top of a cached prefix, and sharing the compute too

blocks.md: Lesson 5 found the cached blocks; this lesson is what the engine does next. Tiny example: a second request has a 7-token prompt whose first 4 tokens hit the cache. Only tokens 4, 5 and 6 go through the model. In every layer their queries must attend to the 4 cached keys and values, read through the block table, plus their own keys and values, which are written into new blocks in the same forward pass.

blocks.title: Which keys each query may attend to (1 = allowed)

scenes.caption: Full prefill of a 7-token prompt: query i attends to keys 0 to i, the causal triangle.
A second request shares tokens 0 to 3 with a cached one. Their rows disappear: no queries, keys or values are computed for them, the cached KV is used instead.
The rectangular part: every new query (positions 4 to 6) reads all 4 cached keys.
The triangular part: new tokens attend causally among themselves. The kernel sees a 3 x 7 problem whose causal mask is shifted right by 4.

blocks.md: One more detail makes the result exact: positions. Many current models, Llama among them, use **RoPE** (rotary position embedding), which rotates pairs of numbers in each query and key by an angle proportional to the token's position, so that a query-key score depends on how far apart the two tokens are. Cached keys were rotated at positions 0 to 3 when they were first computed. The new tokens must be rotated at positions 4 to 6, not restarted at 0, or every distance to a cached key is wrong. The script checks both.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
T, P, D = 7, 4, 8                  # 7 prompt tokens, 4 cached, head dim 8
x = rng.standard_normal((T, D))    # stand-in hidden states
Wq, Wk, Wv = (rng.standard_normal((D, D)) for _ in range(3))

def rope(v, pos):                  # rotate dim pairs by pos * freq
    h = D // 2
    f = pos[:, None] * 10000.0 ** (-np.arange(h) / h)
    c, s = np.cos(f), np.sin(f)
    return np.hstack([v[:, :h] * c - v[:, h:] * s, v[:, :h] * s + v[:, h:] * c])

def attend(q, k, v, mask):
    s = np.where(mask, q @ k.T / np.sqrt(D), -np.inf)
    w = np.exp(s - s.max(1, keepdims=True))
    return (w / w.sum(1, keepdims=True)) @ v

pos = np.arange(T)
full = attend(rope(x @ Wq, pos), rope(x @ Wk, pos), x @ Wv,
              np.tril(np.ones((T, T), bool)))

# second request: tokens 0..3 hit the cache, tokens 4..6 are computed
kc, vc = rope(x[:P] @ Wk, pos[:P]), x[:P] @ Wv     # cached earlier
new = np.arange(P, T)
mask = pos[None, :] <= new[:, None]                # 3 x 7
print(mask.astype(int))
k = np.vstack([kc, rope(x[P:] @ Wk, new)])
v = np.vstack([vc, x[P:] @ Wv])
out = attend(rope(x[P:] @ Wq, new), k, v, mask)
print("max diff vs full prefill:", np.abs(out - full[P:]).max())

# bug: new tokens get positions 0, 1, 2 instead of 4, 5, 6
kb = np.vstack([kc, rope(x[P:] @ Wk, new - P)])
bad = attend(rope(x[P:] @ Wq, new - P), kb, v, mask)
print("positions restarted at 0:", np.abs(bad - full[P:]).max().round(3))
blocks.caption: One attention head with random weights. The test is that prefill on top of the cache reproduces a full prefill, not what the layer computes. Runs with Python 3 and NumPy.

blocks.md: This is the same code path as **chunked prefill**, where a long prompt is computed a chunk per step to share steps with decoding: the second chunk attends to the first chunk's KV exactly as a prefix hit does, it just computed that KV itself one step earlier. vLLM's scheduler makes this explicit. A comment in its source says there is no prefill or decode phase: each request has a count of computed tokens, a prefix hit simply starts that count above zero, and each step schedules tokens to close the gap, which covers chunked prefill, prefix caching and speculative decoding alike.

Two rules decide where a hit ends in vLLM. Hits are whole blocks, so a hit is rounded down to a block boundary and the tokens after it are recomputed even if they were cached. And the last prompt token is always recomputed, because its forward pass yields the logits for the first output token; the hit is capped at the prompt length minus 1 before rounding. A comment in the KV-cache manager notes that this can recompute a whole block rather than one token.

blocks.prompt: Block size 16. A 32-token prompt is sent twice; the first request's 2 blocks are both cached when the second arrives. How many prompt tokens does the second request compute? And for a 33-token prompt sent twice?
blocks.reveal:
**16 and 1.** For 32 tokens the hit is capped at 31, then rounded down to a block boundary: 16 tokens hit, so the whole second block (16 tokens) is recomputed just to get the last token's logits.

For 33 tokens the cap is 32, which is a block boundary, so 32 tokens hit and only token 32 is computed. One extra token cut the recomputed prompt tokens from 16 to 1.

blocks.md:
**Sharing memory is not sharing reads.** Take 32 requests decoding at once over the same 4,000-token prompt, for example parallel samples or many users of one long document. Paged blocks store the prefix once. But each decode step runs attention for 32 queries, and a standard decode kernel handles each request separately: it loads the request's KV, shared blocks included, and does a matrix-vector product with its one query. So the shared prefix is read from GPU memory 32 times per step, per layer.

**Cascade inference** (FlashInfer) and **Hydragen** split attention in two: all 32 queries attend to the shared prefix together, as one matrix-matrix product that loads each prefix tile once, and each query attends to its own suffix separately. The two partial results are merged with the same max-and-sum rescale as lesson 3's partitions.

blocks.title: 32 requests sharing a 4,000-token prefix (Llama 3 8B, BF16)

scenes.caption: KV stored, at 128 KiB per token and 200 private tokens per request: 32 x 4,200 tokens = 16.4 GiB with private copies, 10,400 tokens = 1.27 GiB once the prefix blocks are shared.

KV read per decode step: with plain paged attention each of the 32 queries still loads the whole prefix, 16.4 GiB per step, same as private copies. Cascade reads the prefix once: 1.27 GiB, 12.9x less.

blocks.md: Published measurements (not run here): the FlashInfer blog reports up to 31x faster shared-prefix batch decoding than vLLM's PagedAttention kernel on an H100, and Hydragen reports up to 32x higher end-to-end throughput for CodeLlama-13b, with throughput falling under 15% as the shared prefix grows from 1K to 16K tokens while baselines lose over 90%. Gains need long prefixes and big batches; the FlashInfer course covers the kernels, the merge operator and when cascading does not pay (lesson "Attention states, cascade attention and composable formats").

A common misconception: "the prefix is shared, so it is cheap to decode against". Block sharing saves storage and prefill compute. Decode traffic only drops when the kernel batches the queries that read the shared blocks, as cascade attention does.

A prefix hit turns prefill into a smaller prefill with an offset: new queries see a rectangle of cached keys plus a causal triangle, at positions that continue from the cache. Hits end on block boundaries and never include the last prompt token.

blocks.question: 32 requests share a 4,000-token prompt through shared paged blocks, stored once. During decoding, why does attention still move about 32 prefixes' worth of KV per step?
options: Copy-on-write duplicates the prefix at the first decode step
The block table has to be copied once per request
Each request's query runs its own matrix-vector product, which loads the shared blocks itself; sharing removed duplicate storage, not duplicate reads
Prefix caching is switched off during decoding
blocks.explain: Copy-on-write only copies a shared block that someone writes into, and prefix blocks are full and never written. The shared blocks stay single copies, but a per-request decode kernel reads them once per request. Cascade inference or Hydragen batch the 32 queries against the prefix so it is read once.

blocks.question: An engine computes 3 new tokens on top of a 4-token cached prefix but gives them RoPE positions 0, 1 and 2. What happens?
options: Nothing: positions only matter for the cached tokens
Outputs differ from a full prefill, because the new tokens are rotated as if they started the sequence, so their distances to the cached keys are wrong
The engine detects it and recomputes the prefix
Only the first new token is affected
blocks.explain: RoPE makes a score depend on the distance between query and key positions. The cached keys sit at positions 0 to 3; new tokens at 0 to 2 would look 4 positions closer than they are, so every score changes (the script's 3.4 difference). Nothing crashes, which is what makes the bug dangerous.

lessons.title: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, and when caching pays

blocks.md:
SGLang (Zheng et al., 2023), another open-source serving engine, reached the same goal with a different structure. **RadixAttention** keeps the KV of finished requests, both prompts and generated outputs, in a **radix tree**: a trie whose edges can be labeled with whole token sequences rather than single tokens. Each path from the root spells a cached prefix, and the KV tensors live in a paged pool; in the paper the page size is one token.

A new request walks the tree to find its longest cached prefix, reuses that KV, and inserts the rest as new nodes, splitting an edge when it diverges halfway along it.

blocks.title: A radix tree of cached prefixes evolving over time

scenes.caption: The tree starts empty: nothing is cached.
Chat session 1 sends a system prompt and "Hello!"; the model replies "Hi!". Prompt and output are stored as one edge, one node.
Session 1's second turn starts with the whole first turn, which matches the cached node and is reused. Only the new turn is computed and added as a child.
Session 2 shares only the system prompt. The edge is split at the divergence point so both sessions share the system prompt node.
Memory fills up. The least recently used leaf is evicted first, here session 1's second turn. Ancestors stay reusable until they become leaves themselves.
A few-shot query shares no prefix with anything cached, so it becomes a new child of the root.
A second query with the same examples arrives: the node splits so the examples are shared. While both run, the shared node's reference count is 2 and it cannot be evicted.

blocks.md: As in vLLM, every node has a reference count of running requests and only nodes with count 0 can be evicted. SGLang does not set aside a separate cache region: cached tokens and running requests share one pool, and when enough requests are waiting, the cache shrinks to make room for a bigger batch. The paper measured the tree bookkeeping at 0.2 s out of a 74.3 s run with no reuse at all (under 0.3%), so it is on by default.

blocks.tex: \text{cache hit rate}=\frac{\text{number of cached prompt tokens}}{\text{number of prompt tokens}}
blocks.caption: SGLang's definition. It is what the scheduler tries to maximize.

blocks.md: **Cache-aware scheduling.** The order in which waiting requests run changes the hit rate. Switching back and forth between unrelated prefixes makes them evict each other (thrashing). The SGLang paper sorts waiting requests by matched prefix length, longest first, instead of first come, first served (FCFS); today's SGLang server keeps FCFS as its default and offers this as `--schedule-policy lpm`. The paper proves that for a batch of requests, visiting the radix tree in depth-first order gives the optimal hit rate when the cache holds at least the longest request, and that longest-shared-prefix-first is equivalent to that order.

Why depth-first? The smallest case: A1 and A2 share a 100-token prefix A, B1 and B2 share a prefix B, each request adds 20 tokens of its own, and the cache holds 120 tokens, one request. Every edge of the batch's radix tree must be computed at least once, so 100 + 100 + 4 x 20 = 280 tokens is a floor. FCFS order A1, B1, A2, B2 evicts each prefix just before it is needed again and computes all 480 tokens (0% hits). Depth-first order A1, A2, B1, B2 finishes everything under A while A is cached, then moves to B: 280 tokens, the floor, a 41.7% hit rate. Longest-prefix-first picks A2 right after A1 because its match is 100 tokens against 0 for B1, which is how it ends up depth-first. The SGLang course works through a larger queue and today's scheduler options.

blocks.title: Toy simulation: scheduling order vs prefix hit rate

scenes.caption: Simplified simulation: 8 requests, two groups each sharing a 100-token prefix plus 20 unique tokens, arriving A, B, A, B. With room for only one prefix, FCFS thrashes to 0%; grouping by prefix gets 62.5%.
With room for both prefixes, order no longer matters: 6 of 8 requests reuse 100 of 120 tokens either way (600 / 960 = 62.5%, the most possible here). Scheduling matters when the cache is tight.

blocks.md: Longest-prefix-first can starve a request whose prefix is never cached, since others keep jumping ahead. The SGLang paper says so and leaves fair scheduling as future work.

**Hash table or tree?** Both find the longest cached prefix and both evict LRU with reference counts. vLLM's chained hashes work at block granularity and only cache full blocks; the radix tree in the SGLang paper uses a page size of one token, so a shared prefix is reused right up to the token where it diverges. vLLM's docs note that most open-source engines and many public API endpoints now use some form of prefix caching.

**When does it pay?** Caching skips *prefill* for the matched tokens, which lowers time to first token (TTFT) and frees compute. It does nothing for *decode*: each new token still takes one forward pass. vLLM's docs list long-document question answering and multi-turn chat as big wins, and long answers or prompts with nothing in common as cases with no gain.

The figure below uses the simplest cost model: request time is one minus the hit rate, times the prompt tokens, times the prefill cost per token, plus the output tokens times the decode cost per token. The first term is the time to first token; only it shrinks as the hit rate grows.

blocks.title: Request time vs prefix hit rate (illustrative cost model)

scenes.caption: Made-up costs: 0.25 ms per prefill token, 20 ms per decode token (real prefill cost is not exactly linear). A 4000-token prompt with a 200-token answer: total goes from 5.0 s to 4.1 s at 90% hits. TTFT drops 10x; total only modestly.
Long document, short answer (16000 in, 50 out): prefill dominates, and a 90% hit rate cuts the request from 5.0 s to 1.4 s.
Long answers (1000 out): decode dominates, so even 90% hits only move 21.0 s to 20.1 s. This is the limit the vLLM docs warn about.

blocks.md: Prefix caching never changes outputs. It reuses KV for exactly the same tokens instead of recomputing it, so its effects are on speed and memory (outputs can differ only by the tiny floating-point noise any change in batching causes). It helps exactly as much as prefill dominates the work and prefixes repeat.

blocks.question: Which workload benefits least from prefix caching?
options: A support bot whose 3000-token system prompt is identical for every user
Multi-turn chat where each turn resends the full history
Story generation with short, unique prompts and 2000-token outputs
Many questions asked about the same uploaded report
blocks.explain: Caching only skips prefill for repeated prefixes. Unique short prompts give few hits, and with 2000-token outputs nearly all time is decode, which caching does not touch. The other three resend long identical prefixes.

blocks.question: Why does RadixAttention evict leaves before inner nodes?
options: An inner node is a prefix of every node below it, so evicting it first would make its cached descendants unreachable while their KV still occupies memory
Leaves are always the largest nodes
Inner nodes are stored on the CPU
Leaves always have a nonzero reference count
blocks.explain: A cached suffix is only usable together with its whole prefix. Evicting from the leaves up keeps every remaining node reachable, so shared ancestors such as a system prompt survive as long as anything below them is still cached or they are still in use.

blocks.question: You run a multi-tenant API on vLLM and worry that a user could tell whether a competitor recently sent a given prompt. What does vLLM provide for this?
options: Disable PagedAttention
Set the block size to 1
Switch the hash to xxhash
A per-request cache salt mixed into the first block's hash, so only requests with the same salt share cache
blocks.explain: A shared cache leaks information through time to first token. With `cache_salt`, blocks are only shared within a trust group. A faster non-cryptographic hash like xxhash raises collision risk, which the docs warn can leak data in multi-tenant setups.

lessons.title: Prefix caching across a fleet and behind an API

blocks.md: Everything so far happened inside one engine. Production runs many **replicas** (identical copies of the model server) behind a load balancer, and each replica has its own prefix cache. Tiny example: 4 replicas behind round-robin, one 1,000-token system prompt. The first 4 requests land on 4 different replicas and each computes the prompt, so the fleet pays 4 cold misses where one engine would pay 1. Worse, every replica must keep every popular prompt cached, so the fleet's useful cache is roughly one replica's, not four.

A toy simulation makes the trade-off concrete (Python script, deterministic seed): 400 requests, each a 1,000-token system prompt picked from 8 with skewed popularity (probability 35% for the most popular) plus 100 unique tokens. Three policies:

- **Round-robin**: request i goes to replica i mod 4.
- **Affinity**: go to a replica that has the prompt cached (the least loaded if several do), else to the least-loaded replica. Load is the replica's share of the last 40 requests.
- **Affinity with a cap**: as affinity, but if that replica's load is more than 1.5 times the least-loaded one's, send it to the least-loaded replica instead.

blocks.title: Toy fleet: 4 replicas, 8 system prompts, 400 requests

scenes.caption: Each replica caches 3 prefixes (LRU). Round-robin makes every replica see all 8 prompts, so they keep evicting each other: 50.0% hits. Affinity reaches 89.1%, the most possible here, but its busiest replica takes 38.2% of requests.
Each replica caches all 8 prefixes. Round-robin recovers to 83.6%, paying 4 cold misses per prompt instead of 1. The cap keeps load near 25% at a small hit-rate cost.

blocks.md: Real routers make the same trade between locality and load. Preble's scheduler (Srivatsa et al.) sends a request to the GPU with the longest cached match when the matched prefix is longer than the rest of the prompt, and otherwise picks the GPU with the lowest load cost, counting recent work, the recomputation its evictions would cause, and the new request's own prefill. SGLang's router (sgl-router) keeps a radix tree of each engine's cached prefixes, fed by KV events the engines publish, prefers the engine with the longest match, and gives up locality when that engine fails admission or, in its optional balanced mode, is clearly busier. The llm-d router offers two modes: an **approximate** index that hashes the prompt text in blocks of about 64 tokens (estimated from characters) and assumes the chosen pod now holds them, and a **precise** index fed by **KV events** that vLLM engines publish over ZeroMQ (a messaging library) when blocks are stored or evicted. NVIDIA Dynamo's router likewise scores workers by KV overlap and load, from events or from predictions.

blocks.title: A prefix-aware router in front of four engines

scenes.caption: A request with system prompt S arrives. The router's index has no blocks of S anywhere, so it sends the request to the least-loaded engine, here engine 2.
Engine 2 prefills S and publishes events for the blocks it stored (vLLM's BlockStored, sent over ZeroMQ). The router records which block hashes engine 2 holds.
The next request with S: engine 2 holds the longest matching prefix and its load is fine, so the request goes there and skips the prefill of S.
S becomes popular and engine 2's queue grows. Past a load threshold the router gives up locality and sends S to engine 4, which pays one prefill and becomes a second home for S.
Engine 2 later evicts S under memory pressure and reports it (BlockRemoved). A router that only guesses from its own past decisions would keep sending S there and miss.

blocks.md: An approximate index can be confidently wrong. It records where it sent a prefix, not what the engine still holds, so after an eviction it keeps routing to a replica that will miss. llm-d's docs list exactly this as the approximate mode's weakness; KV events fix it at the cost of more infrastructure. Sending KV between engines instead of recomputing is the KV cache offloading course's subject.

**Behind an API.** Provider prompt caching is the same mechanism sold as a feature. The Anthropic API marks the end of a cacheable prefix with `cache_control` (placed automatically or as explicit breakpoints), needs a minimum prefix length that depends on the model, and never shares caches between organizations. OpenAI caches automatically above a minimum length (newer models also accept explicit breakpoints), and its docs describe a fleet router: requests are routed by load and a hash of the prompt's first tokens, and on older models an optional `prompt_cache_key` helps group related requests, which matters because cached state lives on individual machines.

The engine-level rules explain the advice in both docs: a hit is an exact match from the first token, so put stable content (tools, instructions, documents) first and anything that varies (dates, user names, the question) last. Pricing, TTLs and usage fields are covered in the separate (optional) course on calling LLM APIs at scale (lesson "Caching: skip repeated calls, and reuse repeated prefixes").

blocks.question: Your prompts look like [today's date][user's name][8,000-token product manual][question], and the provider reports almost no cached tokens. What is the best fix?
options: Reorder to [manual][date][name][question] so every request starts with the same 8,000 tokens
Shorten the manual so it fits in one cache block
Ask the provider for a larger block size
Send the manual as a separate request first
blocks.explain: Matching starts at the first token and stops at the first difference, exactly like chained block hashes. A per-request date at the front changes every hash after it, so nothing matches. With the manual first, everything up to the date is a shared prefix.

blocks.md: **Shared caches leak timing.** Lesson 5's `cache_salt` tip has a real-world counterpart. Gu et al. ("Auditing Prompt Caching in Language Model APIs") sent prompts and timed the responses with statistical tests in September and October 2024. They detected prompt caching in 8 of 17 API providers and cache sharing across all users in 7 of them, so an attacker could in principle learn that someone else had sent a prompt with a given prefix from a faster first token. The timing even showed that one embedding model was a decoder-only Transformer. After disclosure, at least five providers made changes such as disabling cache sharing across organizations.

In a fleet the hit rate is decided before any engine sees the request: routing must send a prefix where its KV lives, balanced against load, and the router must learn where KV lives from guesses or from engine events. Cache scope (per user, organization or global) is a privacy decision, not just a performance one.

blocks.question: A router uses an approximate prefix index (it assumes a prefix stays on the replica it was last sent to). Replicas are short on memory and evict often. What do you expect?
options: Hit rates match the router's predictions, because eviction is rare in practice
Outputs become wrong when the router's guess is stale
The router keeps choosing replicas that already evicted the prefix, so predicted hits turn into full prefills and load piles up on those replicas; KV events from the engines would correct the index
Requests fail with an out-of-memory error at the router
blocks.explain: The approximate index tracks routing decisions, not engine state. Under memory pressure the two drift apart: requests are steered toward a replica for a cache it no longer has, paying both the prefill and the locality-driven imbalance. Results stay correct, since a miss just recomputes; only speed suffers.
